pos: n. pr. m. (Hebrew 'Elihu, my God is He)
etymology: Hebrew 'eli, my God, with hu, He — my God is He. The chief bearer is the fourth speaker in Job, the only one God does not rebuke.
biblical_def: The Elihu who matters is the young man who waited while three older friends failed. “Then was kindled the wrath of Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram: against Job was his wrath kindled, because he justified himself rather than God” (Job 32:2). He explains his silence with a courtesy the others had not shown: “I am young, and ye are very old; wherefore I was afraid, and durst not shew you mine opinion” (Job 32:6). Six chapters follow, and their doctrine is high: “The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life” (Job 33:4); “Yea, surely God will not do wickedly, neither will the Almighty pervert judgment” (Job 34:12); “Behold, God exalteth by his power: who teacheth like him?” (Job 36:22). Then the LORD answers out of the whirlwind, and at the end rebukes Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar by name — and says nothing against Elihu. Other men bear the name: an ancestor of Samuel (1Sa 1:1), a captain of Manasseh who joined David at Ziklag (1Ch 12:20), and a Korhite porter (1Ch 26:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not treat Scripture proper names; the sense is Hebrew, 'eli, my God, with hu, He — my God is He.
webster_full: ELIHU. A Hebrew proper name; from eli, my God, and hu, he: my God is he.
WRATH, n. Violent anger; vehement exasperation; indignation.
2. The just indignation of the Supreme Being against sin.
scriptures: Job 32:2
Then was kindled the wrath of Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram: against Job was his wrath kindled, because he justified himself rather than God.
Job 33:4
The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life.
Yea, surely God will not do wickedly, neither will the Almighty pervert judgment.
Behold, God exalteth by his power: who teacheth like him?
corruption_summary: Youth is either dismissed as having nothing to say or flattered as having everything, while Elihu waits for his elders, speaks with reverence, and is the one man in the book God does not correct.
corruption_paragraphs: Elihu is the standing rebuke to both errors about age in the church. He does not assume that being young qualifies him — he waited, he says, because days should speak and multitude of years should teach wisdom. Nor does he conclude that being young disqualifies him: there is a spirit in man, and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding. Great men are not always wise, neither do the aged understand judgment. Both halves are in Job 32, and a church that keeps only one half will produce either contempt for the young or contempt for the old.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what Elihu actually says, since it anticipates the whirlwind. His theme is that God is greater than man, that He speaketh once, yea twice, and that affliction may be chastening rather than sentence. Job's three friends argued from a rule — suffering proves sin — and God calls their speech folly. Elihu argued from God's greatness, and God says nothing against him.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Elihu (H453), my God is He; Buzi, the Buzite, from Buz the son of Nahor; the debate turns on tsadaq (H6663), to justify.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Elihu (H453) — Elihu; Job 32:2, 1 Samuel 1:1, 1 Chronicles 27:18.
Hebrew 'El (H410) — God; the first element of the name.
Hebrew Buzi (H940) — Buzite; of the kindred of Ram, Job 32:2.
Hebrew tsadaq (H6663) — to justify; Job justified himself rather than God.
Hebrew neshamah (H5397) — breath; the breath of the Almighty hath given me life.
usage: “I am young, and ye are very old” — and he had waited to say it.
“The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life” — his ground.
The LORD rebukes three friends by name at the end of the book. Elihu is not among them.

pos: n. pr. m. (Hebrew Chamor, an ass; prince of Shechem)
etymology: Hebrew chamor, a he-ass — a beast of burden and of peace rather than of war. He was the Hivite prince from whose sons Jacob bought his field.
biblical_def: Hamor is the Hivite prince of Shechem, and his name marks both a purchase and a massacre. Jacob dealt honestly with his house: “And he bought a parcel of a field, where he had spread his tent, at the hand of the children of Hamor, Shechem's father, for an hundred pieces of money” (Gen 33:19) — the ground where Joseph's bones were finally buried. Then his son destroyed the peace: “And when Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of the country, saw her, he took her, and lay with her, and defiled her” (Gen 34:2). Hamor came to negotiate: “And Hamor the father of Shechem went out unto Jacob to commune with him” (Gen 34:6), and pleaded his son's case: “The soul of my son Shechem longeth for your daughter: I pray you give her him to wife” (Gen 34:8). Jacob's sons answered deceitfully, required circumcision of every male, and on the third day Simeon and Levi slew them all. Hamor and Shechem died in the city Hamor had ruled, and Jacob's deathbed word on it is not admiration but a curse upon their anger.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not treat Scripture proper names; the sense is Hebrew, chamor, an ass — the common beast of burden in Canaan.
webster_full: HAMOR. A Hebrew proper name; chamor, an ass.
PRINCE, n. In a general sense, a sovereign; the chief and independent ruler of a nation or state.
COMMUNE, v.i. To converse; to talk together familiarly; to impart sentiments mutually.
scriptures: And he bought a parcel of a field, where he had spread his tent, at the hand of the children of Hamor, Shechem's father, for an hundred pieces of money.
Gen 34:2
And when Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of the country, saw her, he took her, and lay with her, and defiled her.
Gen 34:6
And Hamor the father of Shechem went out unto Jacob to commune with him.
Gen 34:8
And Hamor communed with them, saying, The soul of my son Shechem longeth for your daughter: I pray you give her him to wife.
corruption_summary: Genesis 34 is read as either a defence of vengeance or an indictment of Scripture, when the narrative condemns the assault and the massacre alike.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 34 records a rape and a slaughter and endorses neither. Shechem's act is called folly in Israel, a thing which ought not to be done, and the narrative gives Dinah's brothers a real grievance. But Jacob's verdict on Simeon and Levi, delivered on his deathbed and therefore with the weight of a patriarchal oracle, is unsparing: cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel. Scripture's habit of reporting what its heroes did without approving it is the very thing that makes it trustworthy history rather than propaganda.

Hamor himself is the study in expedient fatherhood. His son had committed an atrocity, and the prince came to negotiate a marriage and a trade agreement — make ye marriages with us, and the land shall be before you. Not a word of rebuke to Shechem is recorded. A father who treats his son's grave sin as a diplomatic problem to be managed has already handed him over, and both of them died for it in the gate of their own city.
roots_summary: Hebrew Chamor (H2544), Hamor; from chamor (H2543), an ass; the Hivites (H2340) were among the nations of Canaan.
roots_lines: Hebrew Chamor (H2544) — Hamor; Genesis 33:19, 34:2, 34:6.
Hebrew chamor (H2543) — an ass; the common noun behind the name.
Hebrew Chivvi (H2340) — Hivite; one of the seven nations of Canaan.
Hebrew nebalah (H5039) — folly, disgraceful act; the term Genesis 34:7 uses of Shechem's deed.
Hebrew Shekem (H7927) — Shechem; both the son and the city.
usage: “He bought a parcel of a field… at the hand of the children of Hamor” — and Joseph was buried in it.
“Hamor the father of Shechem went out unto Jacob to commune with him” — to negotiate, not to rebuke.
“The soul of my son Shechem longeth for your daughter” — a father's plea after an atrocity.

pos: n. pr. m. (Hebrew Remalyahu, whom the LORD hath adorned)
etymology: A Hebrew name ending in the covenant name. Remaliah himself does nothing in Scripture; he is known entirely as the father of Pekah, and Isaiah uses that fact as a weapon.
biblical_def: Remaliah is named a dozen times and never acts. He exists in Scripture as a patronymic: Pekah the son of Remaliah. His son was a captain who murdered his king: “But Pekah the son of Remaliah, a captain of his, conspired against him, and smote him in Samaria, in the palace of the king's house… and he killed him, and reigned in his room” (2Ki 15:25). He held the throne twenty years: “In the two and fiftieth year of Azariah king of Judah Pekah the son of Remaliah began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and reigned twenty years” (2Ki 15:27). He allied with Syria against Judah: “In those days the LORD began to send against Judah Rezin the king of Syria, and Pekah the son of Remaliah” (2Ki 15:37). And he died as he had risen: “And Hoshea the son of Elah made a conspiracy against Pekah the son of Remaliah, and smote him, and slew him, and reigned in his stead” (2Ki 15:30). It is that alliance which brought Isaiah to Ahaz with the sign of Immanuel.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not treat Scripture proper names; the sense is Hebrew, a compound with the covenant name — whom the LORD hath adorned.
webster_full: REMALIAH. A Hebrew proper name compounded with Yah, the covenant name of God.
CONSPIRACY, n. A combination of men for an evil purpose; an agreement between two or more persons to commit some crime in concert.
PATRONYMIC, n. A name of men or women derived from that of their parents or ancestors.
scriptures: But Pekah the son of Remaliah, a captain of his, conspired against him, and smote him in Samaria, in the palace of the king's house, with Argob and Arieh, and with him fifty men of the Gileadites: and he killed him, and reigned in his room.
In the two and fiftieth year of Azariah king of Judah Pekah the son of Remaliah began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and reigned twenty years.
And Hoshea the son of Elah made a conspiracy against Pekah the son of Remaliah, and smote him, and slew him, and reigned in his stead, in the twentieth year of Jotham the son of Uzziah.
In those days the LORD began to send against Judah Rezin the king of Syria, and Pekah the son of Remaliah.
corruption_summary: Political alliances are trusted as the real securities of a nation, while Isaiah reduced two allied kings to smoking firebrands and told Ahaz the promise of God was safer.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 7 is where the name Remaliah does its theological work. The prophet is sent to Ahaz while Syria and Israel are marching on Jerusalem, and he refuses to grant Pekah the dignity of a throne name. It is Rezin, and the son of Remaliah — twice, three times, a king reduced to somebody's son. Fear not, Isaiah says, for the two tails of these smoking firebrands. Ahaz would not believe it, sent tribute to Assyria instead, and Assyria came and took the country.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Isaiah's appraisal of raw power. Pekah had murdered his way to a throne, held it twenty years, and terrified a king of Judah. The prophet calls him a smoking firebrand — a stick that has stopped burning — and he was dead within a few years by the same means he had used. The alliance Ahaz preferred to the promise consumed him. Out of that refusal came the sign that a virgin shall conceive.
roots_summary: Hebrew Remalyahu (H7425), whom the LORD hath adorned; Peqach (H6492), Pekah, open-eyed; ben (H1121), son — the word Isaiah leans on.
roots_lines: Hebrew Remalyahu (H7425) — Remaliah; 2 Kings 15:25, 15:27, Isaiah 7:1.
Hebrew Peqach (H6492) — Pekah, his son, king of Israel.
Hebrew qashar (H7194) — to conspire, to bind together; 2 Kings 15:25, 15:30.
Hebrew Retsin (H7526) — Rezin, king of Syria, Pekah's ally.
Hebrew 'Immanu'el (H6005) — Immanuel; the sign given when this alliance threatened Judah.
usage: “Pekah the son of Remaliah, a captain of his, conspired against him” — a throne taken by murder.
“Hoshea the son of Elah made a conspiracy against Pekah” — and lost by the same means.
Isaiah will not say his name: it is Rezin, and the son of Remaliah.

pos: n. pr. m. (Hebrew Kushi, a Cushite, an Ethiopian)
etymology: Hebrew Kush, the land south of Egypt, with the gentilic ending — a man of Cush. The KJV treats it as a name in 2 Samuel and as a patronymic elsewhere.
biblical_def: The Cushi of 2 Samuel is the runner Joab chose to carry the news of Absalom's death, and the scene is one of the most humane in the historical books. “Then said Joab to Cushi, Go tell the king what thou hast seen. And Cushi bowed himself unto Joab, and ran” (2Sa 18:21). Ahimaaz begged to run too and was warned off — “Wherefore wilt thou run, my son, seeing that thou hast no tidings ready?” (2Sa 18:22) — then permitted, and “Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain, and overran Cushi” (2Sa 18:23). Ahimaaz arrived first and could not say it. Cushi arrived second and did: “And, behold, Cushi came; and Cushi said, Tidings, my lord the king: for the LORD hath avenged thee this day of all them that rose up against thee” (2Sa 18:31). Then the king asked the only question he cared about, and Cushi answered it: “The enemies of my lord the king, and all that rise against thee to do thee hurt, be as that young man is” (2Sa 18:32). The name is borne elsewhere by an ancestor of Zephaniah the prophet (Zep 1:1) and of Jehudi in Jeremiah's court (Jer 36:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not treat Scripture proper names; the sense is Hebrew, from Cush, the region south of Egypt — an Ethiopian.
webster_full: CUSHI. A Hebrew proper name; from Cush, a Cushite or Ethiopian.
ETHIOPIAN, n. A native of Ethiopia; a blackamoor.
TIDINGS, n. plu. News; advice; information; intelligence; account of what has taken place.
scriptures: Then said Joab to Cushi, Go tell the king what thou hast seen. And Cushi bowed himself unto Joab, and ran.
But howsoever, said he, let me run. And he said unto him, Run. Then Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain, and overran Cushi.
And, behold, Cushi came; and Cushi said, Tidings, my lord the king: for the LORD hath avenged thee this day of all them that rose up against thee.
And the king said unto Cushi, Is the young man Absalom safe? And Cushi answered, The enemies of my lord the king, and all that rise against thee to do thee hurt, be as that young man is.
corruption_summary: Bad news is softened until it says nothing, while Cushi answered the king's actual question and Ahimaaz, who ran faster, could not.
corruption_paragraphs: The contrast between the two runners is the whole lesson. Ahimaaz was the priest's son, he was fast, he insisted on going, and when he stood before David he reported a victory and then said, I saw a great tumult, but I knew not what it was. He had the speed and not the message. Cushi came behind and told the king plainly what he did not want to hear. Ministry that arrives first with nothing to say is not superior to ministry that arrives late with the truth.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture's idea of faithfulness in speech includes the delivery of unbearable news. Cushi did not soften it, and he did not enjoy it; he framed it as a wish upon the king's enemies, which was as gentle as truth allowed. David's answer — O my son Absalom, would God I had died for thee — is what the truth cost, and the messenger bore it rather than sparing himself.
roots_summary: Hebrew Kushi (H3569), a Cushite; from Kush (H3568), the son of Ham and the land named for him; the KJV renders the gentilic as a personal name in 2 Samuel 18.
roots_lines: Hebrew Kushi (H3569) — Cushi, a Cushite; 2 Samuel 18:21, Zephaniah 1:1.
Hebrew Kush (H3568) — Cush; Genesis 10:6, the son of Ham.
Hebrew basar (H1319) — to bear tidings, to publish good news; the runner's office.
Hebrew ruts (H7323) — to run; Ahimaaz overran Cushi.
Hebrew naqam (H5358) — to avenge; the LORD hath avenged thee this day.
usage: “Go tell the king what thou hast seen” — the whole commission.
“Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain, and overran Cushi” — and arrived with nothing.
“Be as that young man is” — the answer David asked for and could not bear.

pos: n. pr. m. (Hebrew Yerachme'el, God will have mercy)
etymology: Hebrew racham, to have compassion, with 'El, God — God will have mercy. The chief bearer is Hezron's firstborn, whose line the Chronicler traces at unusual length.
biblical_def: Jerahmeel means God will have mercy, and the man who bore it heads a long and otherwise unremarkable branch of Judah. “The sons also of Hezron, that were born unto him; Jerahmeel, and Ram, and Chelubai” (1Ch 2:9). His household is then set out with a care the Chronicler rarely spends outside the royal line: “And the sons of Jerahmeel the firstborn of Hezron were, Ram the firstborn, and Bunah, and Oren, and Ozem, and Ahijah” (1Ch 2:25); “Jerahmeel had also another wife, whose name was Atarah; she was the mother of Onam” (1Ch 2:26); “And the sons of Ram the firstborn of Jerahmeel were, Maaz, and Jamin, and Eker” (1Ch 2:27), running on to “These were the sons of Jerahmeel” (1Ch 2:33). The Jerahmeelites lived in the Negeb south of Judah, and David sent them spoil from Ziklag. Two other men bear the name: a Levite of Kish's house (1Ch 24:29), and one of the three officers Jehoiakim sent to arrest Baruch and Jeremiah (Jer 36:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not treat Scripture proper names; the sense is Hebrew, from racham, to have mercy, and 'El, God — God will have mercy.
webster_full: JERAHMEEL. A Hebrew proper name; from racham, to have compassion, and El, God: God will have mercy.
MERCY, n. That benevolence, mildness or tenderness of heart which disposes a person to overlook injuries, or to treat an offender better than he deserves.
COMPASSION, n. A suffering with another; pity; commiseration.
scriptures: The sons also of Hezron, that were born unto him; Jerahmeel, and Ram, and Chelubai.
And the sons of Jerahmeel the firstborn of Hezron were, Ram the firstborn, and Bunah, and Oren, and Ozem, and Ahijah.
Jerahmeel had also another wife, whose name was Atarah; she was the mother of Onam.
And the sons of Jonathan; Peleth, and Zaza. These were the sons of Jerahmeel.
corruption_summary: God's mercy is imagined as a general disposition, while the Hebrew word behind this name is drawn from the womb and always attaches to particular people.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what the name assumes. Racham, the root, is the same word as the womb — the mercy of God in Hebrew is visceral and particular, the compassion of a mother for the child of her body. Isaiah 49:15 argues from exactly there: can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? A man named Jerahmeel carried that claim as his own name in a branch of Judah that produced no king and no prophet.

The Chronicler's attention to this line is itself the doctrine. He is writing after the exile to a diminished people, and he spends most of a chapter on the household of a firstborn whose descendants lived at the edge of the desert. God will have mercy — on the main line and on the branch, on the famous house and on the obscure one. Chronicles is the book that insists the register is not a ranking.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yerachme'el (H3396), God will have mercy; from racham (H7355), to have compassion, cognate with rechem (H7358), the womb.
roots_lines: Hebrew Yerachme'el (H3396) — Jerahmeel; 1 Chronicles 2:9, 2:25, Jeremiah 36:26.
Hebrew racham (H7355) — to have compassion, to love deeply.
Hebrew rechem (H7358) — womb; the same consonants, the root image of mercy.
Hebrew rachamim (H7356) — tender mercies; the plural, used of God throughout the Psalms.
Hebrew Chetsron (H2696) — Hezron; his father, in the line of Pharez and of Christ.
usage: “Jerahmeel the firstborn of Hezron” — a firstborn with no crown.
“These were the sons of Jerahmeel” — a branch recorded at length for its own sake.
The name is a promise: God will have mercy.

pos: n. pr. m. (Hebrew Shaphat, he hath judged)
etymology: Hebrew shaphat, to judge — the verb behind shophetim, Judges, and behind Jehoshaphat, the LORD hath judged. The chief bearer is the father of Elisha.
biblical_def: Shaphat means he hath judged, and the man Scripture names most often is a farmer of Abelmeholah whose son inherited Elijah's mantle. The LORD names him to Elijah at Horeb: “And Jehu the son of Nimshi shalt thou anoint to be king over Israel: and Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abelmeholah shalt thou anoint to be prophet in thy room” (1Ki 19:16). Elisha is identified by his father throughout his ministry — when Jehoshaphat sought a prophet in the wilderness of Edom: “Here is Elisha the son of Shaphat, which poured water on the hands of Elijah” (2Ki 3:11), and when the king of Israel swore to have his head in besieged Samaria: “God do so and more also to me, if the head of Elisha the son of Shaphat shall stand on him this day” (2Ki 6:31). Another Shaphat was the spy sent from Simeon: “Of the tribe of Simeon, Shaphat the son of Hori” (Num 13:5) — one of the ten who brought back an evil report.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not treat Scripture proper names; the sense is Hebrew, from shaphat, to judge — he hath judged.
webster_full: SHAPHAT. A Hebrew proper name; from shaphat, to judge: he hath judged.
JUDGE, v.t. To compare facts or ideas, and perceive their agreement or disagreement; to hear and determine, as in a court of law.
MANTLE, n. A kind of cloak or loose garment worn over other garments.
scriptures: Num 13:5
Of the tribe of Simeon, Shaphat the son of Hori.
And Jehu the son of Nimshi shalt thou anoint to be king over Israel: and Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abelmeholah shalt thou anoint to be prophet in thy room.

But Jehoshaphat said, Is there not here a prophet of the LORD, that we may enquire of the LORD by him? And one of the king of Israel's servants answered and said, Here is Elisha the son of Shaphat, which poured water on the hands of Elijah.
Then he said, God do so and more also to me, if the head of Elisha the son of Shaphat shall stand on him this day.
corruption_summary: A call to ministry is imagined as an escape from ordinary work, while the LORD found Elisha the son of Shaphat behind twelve yoke of oxen and took him from the plough.
corruption_paragraphs: Shaphat of Abelmeholah was a substantial farmer — his son was ploughing with twelve yoke of oxen when Elijah passed by and cast his mantle upon him. Elisha asked leave to kiss his father and mother, then took a yoke of oxen, slew them, boiled their flesh with the instruments of the oxen, gave it to the people, and went after Elijah. He burned the plough. The call did not come to a man waiting in a school of the prophets; it came to a man at work, and it cost him a business.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture keeps the father's name attached to the prophet for forty years. Elisha the son of Shaphat is how the king of Israel curses him and how the servant commends him. A man's calling does not erase his household; it is carried out under his own name and his father's, in public, where both can be held to account.
roots_summary: Hebrew Shaphat (H8202), he hath judged; from shaphat (H8199), to judge; the same root in shophet, judge, and Yehoshaphat, the LORD hath judged.
roots_lines: Hebrew Shaphat (H8202) — Shaphat; Numbers 13:5, 1 Kings 19:16, 2 Kings 6:31.
Hebrew shaphat (H8199) — to judge, to govern; the verb of the book of Judges.
Hebrew 'Elisha' (H477) — Elisha, God is salvation; his son.
Hebrew 'addereth (H155) — mantle; what Elijah cast upon him.
Hebrew 'Abel Mecholah (H65) — Abelmeholah, the meadow of dancing; Shaphat's home.
usage: “Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abelmeholah shalt thou anoint to be prophet in thy room” — named at Horeb.
“Which poured water on the hands of Elijah” — the credential that mattered.
“If the head of Elisha the son of Shaphat shall stand on him this day” — cursed by his father's name.

pos: n. pr. m. (Hebrew Ye'ush, he will gather, or assembler)
etymology: A Hebrew name from a root meaning to gather or hasten to help. The first bearer is a son of Esau and a duke of Edom.
biblical_def: Jeush first appears as a son of Esau by his Canaanite wife: “And Aholibamah bare Jeush, and Jaalam, and Korah: these are the sons of Esau, which were born unto him in the land of Canaan” (Gen 36:5). The record is repeated, “and she bare to Esau Jeush, and Jaalam, and Korah” (Gen 36:14), and then he is given a title: “And these are the sons of Aholibamah Esau's wife; duke Jeush, duke Jaalam, duke Korah” (Gen 36:18). The Chronicler repeats the line at the head of his history: “The sons of Esau; Eliphaz, Reuel, and Jeush, and Jaalam, and Korah” (1Ch 1:35). Other men bear it: a Benjamite of Bilhan's house (1Ch 7:10), a Levite of the sons of Shimei whose small household was reckoned as one (1Ch 23:11), and a son of Rehoboam whom his father set with his brethren in the fenced cities of Judah (2Ch 11:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not treat Scripture proper names; the sense is Hebrew, from a root meaning to gather or to hasten to help.
webster_full: JEUSH. A Hebrew proper name; from a root signifying to assemble or hasten together.
DUKE, n. In Great Britain, one of the highest order of nobility; in Scripture, the chief of a family or tribe.
GATHER, v.t. To bring together; to collect a number of separate things.
scriptures: Gen 36:5
And Aholibamah bare Jeush, and Jaalam, and Korah: these are the sons of Esau, which were born unto him in the land of Canaan.
And these were the sons of Aholibamah, the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon, Esau's wife: and she bare to Esau Jeush, and Jaalam, and Korah.
And these are the sons of Aholibamah Esau's wife; duke Jeush, duke Jaalam, duke Korah: these were the dukes that came of Aholibamah the daughter of Anah, Esau's wife.
The sons of Esau; Eliphaz, Reuel, and Jeush, and Jaalam, and Korah.
corruption_summary: Esau's line is treated as an afterthought, while Genesis gives it a full chapter and the New Testament makes it the standing case for election.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 36 is a whole chapter of dukes, and Jeush is one of them. Esau had lands, cities, chiefs and kings that reigned in Edom before there reigned any king over the children of Israel, while Jacob's house was still a wandering family. Scripture records the prosperity without embarrassment. Worldly success is not evidence of divine favour, and Genesis proves it by giving the rejected brother the more impressive genealogy.

Paul takes exactly this material for the sharpest statement of unconditional election in the canon: the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, it was said, The elder shall serve the younger. As it is written, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated. The dukes of Edom are not an interruption in the covenant story; they are the visible half of the doctrine, and the doctrine is that God's choice does not answer to what men can see.
roots_summary: Hebrew Ye'ush (H3266), assembler; 'alluph (H441), duke or chief of a clan; 'Edom (H123), red, the nation of Esau.
roots_lines: Hebrew Ye'ush (H3266) — Jeush; Genesis 36:5, 36:14, 1 Chronicles 1:35.
Hebrew 'alluph (H441) — duke, chief; the title given him in Genesis 36:18.
Hebrew 'Oholibamah (H173) — Aholibamah, his mother, Esau's Canaanite wife.
Hebrew 'Esav (H6215) — Esau; the brother whose line Genesis 36 records.
Hebrew 'Edom (H123) — Edom, red; the nation descended from him.
usage: “These are the sons of Esau, which were born unto him in the land of Canaan” — and Genesis names them all.
“Duke Jeush, duke Jaalam, duke Korah” — titles Jacob's sons did not yet have.
A chapter of Edomite nobility, recorded without envy and without approval.

pos: n. pr. m. (Hebrew 'Ebed-melek, servant of the king; an Ethiopian eunuch in Zedekiah's house)
etymology: Hebrew 'ebed, servant, and melek, king — servant of the king. Whether a name or an office title, the man it belonged to served a higher King than Zedekiah.
biblical_def: Ebedmelech is the Ethiopian eunuch who saved Jeremiah's life. The princes had cast the prophet into a cistern to die: they let him down with cords, and in the dungeon there was no water, but mire, so Jeremiah sunk in the mire (Jer 38:6). Then: “Now when Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, one of the eunuchs which was in the king's house, heard that they had put Jeremiah in the dungeon; the king then sitting in the gate of Benjamin” (Jer 38:7). He did not send word. “Ebedmelech went forth out of the king's house, and spake to the king” (Jer 38:8), telling Zedekiah plainly that these men had done evil. The king relented: “Then the king commanded Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, saying, Take from hence thirty men with thee, and take up Jeremiah the prophet out of the dungeon, before he die” (Jer 38:10). And the rescue is recorded with a tenderness the book rarely allows: “So Ebedmelech took the men with him, and went into the house of the king under the treasury, and took thence old cast clouts and old rotten rags, and let them down by cords into the dungeon to Jeremiah” (Jer 38:11), telling him to put them under his armholes so the ropes would not cut him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not treat Scripture proper names; the sense is Hebrew, 'ebed, servant, and melek, king — the king's servant.
webster_full: EBEDMELECH. A Hebrew proper name; from ebed, a servant, and melech, a king: the king's servant.
EUNUCH, n. A male of the human species castrated; among Oriental courts, an officer of the household.
CLOUT, n. A patch; a piece of cloth or leather to cover a hole, or for mending.
scriptures: Jer 38:7
Now when Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, one of the eunuchs which was in the king's house, heard that they had put Jeremiah in the dungeon; the king then sitting in the gate of Benjamin;
Jer 38:8
Ebedmelech went forth out of the king's house, and spake to the king, saying,
Then the king commanded Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, saying, Take from hence thirty men with thee, and take up Jeremiah the prophet out of the dungeon, before he die.

So Ebedmelech took the men with him, and went into the house of the king under the treasury, and took thence old cast clouts and old rotten rags, and let them down by cords into the dungeon to Jeremiah.
corruption_summary: Courage is imagined as a native temperament, while Jeremiah 39 tells Ebedmelech the reason he will be spared is that he put his trust in the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: Every human factor was against this rescue. Ebedmelech was a foreigner, a eunuch — a man the law barred from the congregation — and a servant in a court where the princes had just demonstrated they could kill a prophet without consequence. He had no standing to speak and every reason to keep his position. He walked out to the gate of Benjamin and told the king his officers had done evil, and then went for the rags himself.

Jeremiah 39:16–18 gives the LORD's own verdict, delivered before Jerusalem fell: I will deliver thee in that day, and thou shalt not be given into the hand of the men of whom thou art afraid… because thou hast put thy trust in me, saith the LORD. Note the phrase of whom thou art afraid. He was afraid, and he went anyway, and God calls that trust. The Ethiopian who saved Jeremiah stands with the Ethiopian of Acts 8 as Scripture's answer to any reading of the covenant that makes it a matter of blood.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Ebed-melek (H5663), servant of the king; 'ebed (H5650), servant; saris (H5631), eunuch or court officer; Kushi (H3569), Ethiopian.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Ebed-melek (H5663) — Ebedmelech; Jeremiah 38:7, 38:10, 39:16.
Hebrew 'ebed (H5650) — servant, bondman; the first element of the name.
Hebrew saris (H5631) — eunuch, chamberlain; his position in Zedekiah's house.
Hebrew bor (H953) — pit, dungeon, cistern; where Jeremiah sank in the mire.
Hebrew batach (H982) — to trust; the reason the LORD gives for sparing him.
usage: “Ebedmelech went forth out of the king's house, and spake to the king” — he did not send word.
“Take up Jeremiah the prophet out of the dungeon, before he die” — the king's order, given to him.
“Old cast clouts and old rotten rags” — so the cords would not cut the prophet's arms.

pos: n. pr. m. (Hebrew 'Oholi'ab, tent of the father; the craftsman of Dan)
etymology: Hebrew 'ohel, tent, and 'ab, father — the father's tent. A fitting name for the man the LORD appointed to help build His.
biblical_def: Aholiab is Bezaleel's partner in building the tabernacle, and the LORD names him personally. “And I, behold, I have given with him Aholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan: and in the hearts of all that are wise hearted I have put wisdom, that they may make all that I have commanded thee” (Exo 31:6). He was gifted not only to work but to train others: “And he hath put in his heart that he may teach, both he, and Aholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan” (Exo 35:34). The work then proceeded: “Then wrought Bezaleel and Aholiab, and every wise hearted man, in whom the LORD put wisdom and understanding to know how to work all manner of work for the service of the sanctuary, according to all that the LORD had commanded” (Exo 36:1), and Moses summoned them: “And Moses called Bezaleel and Aholiab, and every wise hearted man, in whose heart the LORD had put wisdom, even every one whose heart stirred him up to come unto the work to do it” (Exo 36:2). His trades are listed at the close of the account: an engraver, and a cunning workman, and an embroiderer in blue, and in purple, and in scarlet, and fine linen (Exo 38:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not treat Scripture proper names; the sense is Hebrew, 'ohel, a tent, and 'ab, father — the father's tent.
webster_full: AHOLIAB. A Hebrew proper name; from ohel, a tent, and ab, a father: the father's tent.
EMBROIDER, v.t. To border with ornamental needle-work, or figures.
CUNNING, a. Knowing; skilful; experienced; well-instructed. It is applied in Scripture to artificers, as a cunning workman.
scriptures: Exo 31:6

And I, behold, I have given with him Aholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan: and in the hearts of all that are wise hearted I have put wisdom, that they may make all that I have commanded thee;
And he hath put in his heart that he may teach, both he, and Aholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan.
Exo 36:1

Then wrought Bezaleel and Aholiab, and every wise hearted man, in whom the LORD put wisdom and understanding to know how to work all manner of work for the service of the sanctuary, according to all that the LORD had commanded.
Exo 36:2
And Moses called Bezaleel and Aholiab, and every wise hearted man, in whose heart the LORD had put wisdom, even every one whose heart stirred him up to come unto the work to do it:
corruption_summary: Skilled work is treated as secular and only preaching as spiritual, while Exodus records the LORD naming two craftsmen and filling them with His Spirit for the job.
corruption_paragraphs: The first men in Scripture said to be filled with the Spirit of God are not prophets or priests but a jeweller and an embroiderer. Bezaleel of Judah and Aholiab of Dan — and the tribes matter, since Judah is the royal tribe and Dan the one that would give Israel its worst idolatry. The LORD named them both by name to Moses before either had cut a stone. Any doctrine of vocation that ranks the pulpit above the workbench has to explain Exodus 31.

Exodus 35:34 adds the detail most easily missed: God put it in his heart that he may teach. Aholiab was gifted to reproduce his skill in others, not merely to exercise it. A craftsman who trains no one has kept half his gift. The tabernacle was built by a workforce of wise hearted men whose competence came, the text says twice, from the LORD putting wisdom in their hearts — and two named men were charged with getting it into them.

Hebrew Dan (H1835) — Dan; his tribe, set beside royal Judah in the work.
usage: “I have given with him Aholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan” — named by the LORD.
“He hath put in his heart that he may teach” — the gift includes reproducing it.
“Every one whose heart stirred him up to come unto the work” — called, and willing.

pos: n. pr. m. (Hebrew Neriyah, the LORD is my lamp)
etymology: Hebrew ner, lamp, with Yah — the LORD is my lamp, the confession of 2 Samuel 22:29. He is known as the father of Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe.
biblical_def: Neriah appears in Scripture only as a father, and his son held the pen for the greatest prophecy of the exile. At the purchase of the field in Anathoth, when Jerusalem was already surrounded: “And I gave the evidence of the purchase unto Baruch the son of Neriah, the son of Maaseiah, in the sight of Hanameel mine uncle's son” (Jer 32:12), and “Now when I had delivered the evidence of the purchase unto Baruch the son of Neriah, I prayed unto the LORD” (Jer 32:16). When the LORD commanded the whole prophecy written: “Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah: and Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the LORD, which he had spoken unto him, upon a roll of a book” (Jer 36:4). And Baruch read it publicly at cost: “And Baruch the son of Neriah did according to all that Jeremiah the prophet commanded him, reading in the book the words of the LORD in the LORD'S house” (Jer 36:8). Jehoiakim burned that roll leaf by leaf on the hearth, and Baruch wrote it again. Another son of Neriah, Seraiah, carried Jeremiah's word against Babylon to Babylon itself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not treat Scripture proper names; the sense is Hebrew, ner, a lamp, with Yah, the LORD — the LORD is my lamp.
webster_full: NERIAH. A Hebrew proper name; from ner, a lamp or candle, and Yah, the LORD: the LORD is my lamp.
LAMP, n. A vessel with a wick, used for the combustion of inflammable liquids for the purpose of producing light.
SCRIBE, n. A writer; a notary; one who writes for another; in Scripture, a secretary.
scriptures: And I gave the evidence of the purchase unto Baruch the son of Neriah, the son of Maaseiah, in the sight of Hanameel mine uncle's son, and in the presence of the witnesses that subscribed the book of the purchase, before all the Jews that sat in the court of the prison.
Now when I had delivered the evidence of the purchase unto Baruch the son of Neriah, I prayed unto the LORD, saying,
Jer 36:4
Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah: and Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the LORD, which he had spoken unto him, upon a roll of a book.
Jer 36:8
And Baruch the son of Neriah did according to all that Jeremiah the prophet commanded him, reading in the book the words of the LORD in the LORD'S house.
corruption_summary: Scripture is treated as a text that assembled itself over centuries, while Jeremiah 36 records the dictation, the scribe, the destruction of the roll and its rewriting by name.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 36 is the most detailed account of the production of a book of Scripture anywhere in the canon, and every stage is attributed. The LORD commands; Jeremiah dictates; Baruch the son of Neriah writes; Baruch reads it in the LORD's house; Jehudi reads it to the king; the king cuts it with a penknife and burns it; and the LORD commands another roll, to which were added besides unto them many like words. Verbal inspiration is not a doctrine imposed on this chapter from outside. It is the chapter's own account of itself.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour due to the man who holds the pen. Baruch is named more than a dozen times, always as the son of Neriah, and Jeremiah 45 records a personal word from the LORD to him alone when he was weary of it. God did not overlook the scribe. Neither should the church, whose Scriptures reached it through the hands of copyists whose names are mostly lost.
roots_summary: Hebrew Neriyah (H5374), the LORD is my lamp; from ner (H5216), lamp, and Yah (H3050); his son is Baruk (H1263), blessed.

usage: “Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the LORD” — dictation, attributed.
“Reading in the book the words of the LORD in the LORD'S house” — and it cost him.
The name means the LORD is my lamp; his son wrote by one, in a burning city.
